keyVerseText: And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.
rootMeaning: The word גְּבִירָה (gᵉbîyrâh) is the feminine form of גְּבִיר (gᵉbîyr), which means 'lord' or 'master.' This etymological connection highlights that גְּבִירָה literally signifies a female ruler or lady of authority, emphasizing her position as a sovereign or a person of high status. The root meaning conveys more than just the English term 'queen' by underscoring her role as a master or ruler in her own right, not merely a consort.
usageInScripture: The term גְּבִירָה appears six times in Scripture, consistently translated with reference to 'queen' or 'queen-mother.' The top translations such as 'the queen,' 'from being queen,' and 'queen-mother' indicate its use both for a reigning queen and specifically for the queen-mother, a position of significant influence. This consistency in translation reveals that גְּבִירָה denotes a woman exercising recognized authority, often connected to royal lineage and governance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גְּבִירָה as a title for a queen or queen-mother enriches our grasp of biblical leadership structures and the God-ordained order within the monarchy. It reflects the dignity and authority given to women in certain roles of governance, pointing to God's sovereign design in human institutions. This term also foreshadows the ultimate Queen in Christian theology—Christ's bride and the Church, who shares in His reign. Recognizing the authority embedded in גְּבִירָה encourages believers to honor God-ordained leadership and to see the value of faithful stewardship within the household of faith.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 11:19, the word גְּבִירָה appears in the phrase 'Tahpenes the queen,' identifying her as a woman of high rank and influence, the sister of Pharaoh's wife. This usage highlights the respect and status accorded to her, reinforcing the idea of גְּבִירָה as a recognized royal authority. The verse shows how this title connects to real historical figures, grounding the biblical narrative in a context of recognized leadership and favor.
